intro: The third conditional (If I had known, I would have come) imagines a different past: what would have happened if things had gone differently. We use it to express regret, criticism and relief, and to analyse mistakes.
objectifs: Build the third conditional with if + past perfect and would have + past participle.
Recognise and use the contracted forms ('d = had / 'd = would, would've) in speech.
Express regret, criticism and relief about the past.
Add meaning with could have and might have, and tell the three conditionals apart.

texte: Condition: if + past perfect (had + participle). Result: would have + past participle. Both parts are about the past, and about something that did not happen.
The classic mistake is to put would in the if-clause: “If I would have known” is wrong in standard English, even if you sometimes hear it in casual American speech.

lignes: I didn't know, so I didn't come.
If we hadn't missed the bus,
We missed the bus; we were late.
the match would have taken place.
It rained; the match was cancelled.

texte: In speech, we contract almost everything: “If I'd known, I'd have come.” The first 'd = had (followed by a participle); the second 'd = would (followed by have).
Would have sounds like /ˈwʊdəv/ and is sometimes written would've. Never write “would of”: it's a common mistake, even among native speakers, because 've and of sound the same /əv/.
exemples: If you'd told me, I'd have helped you.
= If you had told me, I would have helped you.
She would've loved this place.
Would've = would have (informal writing).
If they'd left earlier, they wouldn't have missed the flight.
Negative: wouldn't have.

texte: Regret (about yourself): “If I had studied harder, I would have got a better job.” Criticism (of someone else): “If you had listened to me, this wouldn't have happened!” Relief (luckily…): “If the doctor hadn't come so quickly, he would have died.”
The third conditional also helps to analyse causes, for example at work: “If we had tested the software, the client wouldn't have complained.”
exemples: If I'd taken the job in Toronto, I would have earned more.
Regret.
If you had checked the address, we wouldn't have got lost.
Criticism.
If she hadn't worn a helmet, she would have been badly hurt.
Relief.

texte: In the result: could have + participle = it would have been possible; might have + participle = perhaps it would have happened. “If you had asked me, I could have helped you” / “If we had left earlier, we might have caught the train.”
In the condition, could have is not possible: use had been able to. “If I had been able to come, I would have come.”

lignes: If he'd trained, he would have won.
If he'd trained, he could have won.
he would have been able to
If he'd trained, he might have won.
If he'd trained, he wouldn't have lost.

exemples: If I had been able to come, I would have come.
In the condition: had been able to (not could have).
You could have told me earlier!
Criticism with could have, without if.

sections.titre: The three conditionals side by side
texte: First: possible future (if + present, will). Second: imaginary present or future (if + past, would). Third: imaginary past (if + past perfect, would have). Each time, we move one tense back.
We can mix the second and third when a past cause has a present result: “If I had taken the medicine, I would feel better now.” This mixed conditional is studied at B2 (lesson 158).

lignes: If I see Ali, I'll tell him.
If I saw Ali, I'd tell him.
If I had seen Ali, I'd have told him.

exemples: If I had taken the medicine, I would feel better now.
Past cause, present result (mixed conditional).
If I had seen Ali, I'd have told him the news.
Third conditional: I didn't see him.

formule: If + had + participle, would / could / might have + participle (If I had known, I would have come.)
prononciation: would have reduces to /ˈwʊdəv/ or even /ˈwʊdə/ in fast speech: “I'd have come” /aɪd əv ˈkʌm/.
wouldn't have: /ˈwʊdntəv/, three syllables joined together.
had is weak and often contracted: “If I'd known” /ɪf aɪd ˈnəʊn/. The 'd is light but necessary.
In criticism, the key word gets strong stress: “If you had LISTENED to me…”
could have /ˈkʊdəv/ and should have /ˈʃʊdəv/ follow the same pattern (never write “could of”).
erreurs: If I would have known, I would have come.
If I had known, I would have come.
Past perfect in the if-clause, never would have.
If I had known, I would come.
If I had known, I would have come.
For a past result: would have + participle.
If she had studied, she would have pass.
If she had studied, she would have passed.
After would have, use the past participle.
I would have helped you. / I'd have helped you.
If I knew, I would have told you.
If I had known, I would have told you.
Past situation: had known, not knew.
If we had left earlier, we could caught the train.
If we had left earlier, we could have caught the train.
Could have + participle for a past possibility.

dialogue.contexte: Brussels, after a bad job interview. Inès talks on the phone with her sister Mariam, in Dakar.
lignes: So, how did the interview go?
Badly. If I'd known they wanted a presentation, I would have prepared one.
Didn't they tell you in the email?
They did, but I didn't read it carefully. If I had read it, I wouldn't have been so surprised.
Well, if you'd called me, I could have helped you prepare.
I know. And if the train hadn't been late, I might have had time to calm down.
Don't worry. You've learnt something. Next time you'll be ready.
Back to the present and future.
You're right. If I get another interview, I'll read everything twice!

mots: regret
I regret not taking that job.
to feel sorry about something you did or didn't do
mistake
If I hadn't made that mistake, we would have won.
something that is wrong
fortunately
Fortunately, someone had called an ambulance.
luckily
blame
Don't blame me! If you had checked, it wouldn't have happened.
to say that someone is responsible for something bad
avoid
We could have avoided the problem.
to stop something bad from happening
hindsight
With hindsight, I would have chosen a different course.
understanding a situation only after it has happened
opportunity
If I'd had the opportunity, I would have studied abroad.
a chance to do something
accident
If he had driven more slowly, the accident wouldn't have happened.
something bad that happens by chance, e.g. a car crash
warn
If you had warned me, I would have stayed at home.
to tell someone about a possible danger or problem

items: If I had known about the party, I would have gone.
I didn't know about the party, so I didn't go.
If she hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have been late.
She missed the bus, so she was late.
If they had saved money, they could have bought a house.
They didn't save money, so they couldn't buy a house.
If it hadn't snowed, the flight wouldn't have been cancelled.
It snowed, so the flight was cancelled.

exercices.titre: 2. Put the verbs in the right form
exercices.consigne: Put the verbs in the third conditional.
items: If you ___ (ask) me, I ___ (help) you.
had asked … would have helped
We ___ (not / get) lost if we ___ (take) a map.
wouldn't have got … had taken
If he ___ (not / eat) that fish, he ___ (not / be) ill.
hadn't eaten … wouldn't have been
If I ___ (have) your number, I ___ (call) you.
had had … would have called
She ___ (might / win) if she ___ (train) more.
might have won … had trained

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence in the third conditional.
items: I didn't set my alarm, so I overslept.
If I had set my alarm, I wouldn't have overslept.
You didn't tell me, so I didn't come.
If you had told me, I would have come.
The shop was closed, so we didn't buy any bread.
If the shop hadn't been closed, we would have bought some bread.
He forgot his passport, so he missed the flight.
If he hadn't forgotten his passport, he wouldn't have missed the flight.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: If I would have seen you, I would have said hello.
If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
If they had come, they would enjoy the concert.
If they had come, they would have enjoyed the concert.
I would of called you, but my phone was dead.
I would have called you, but my phone was dead.
If she had went to the doctor, she would have felt better.
If she had gone to the doctor, she would have felt better.

exercices.consigne: Write a third conditional sentence for each situation.
items: You didn't know about the party, so you didn't come. Explain.
If I had known, I would have come.
Your friend didn't listen to you, and there was a problem. Criticise him.
If you had listened to me, this wouldn't have happened.
You left late and missed the beginning of the film. Say what was possible.
If we had left earlier, we could have seen the beginning of the film.
Your friend didn't ask her. Maybe she would have said yes.
She might have accepted if you had asked her.

exercices.consigne: Think of an important decision in your life. Write 4 third conditional sentences to imagine what would have happened otherwise (would have, could have, might have).
items: Example answer

If I hadn't moved to Montreal, I wouldn't have met my wife. If I had stayed in Douala, I might have opened a business with my brother. I could have become an engineer if I had chosen maths at university. But if I hadn't made those choices, I wouldn't have this life, and I love it.

a_retenir: If + past perfect, would have + participle: an imaginary past that didn't happen.
Never would have in the if-clause.
'd = had before a participle; 'd = would before have.
could have = it was possible; might have = perhaps.
Write would have / would've, never “would of”.
